name: Alasdair Worrell
project: Monitoring ecological restoration and biodiversity in the Scottish uplands using uncrewed aerial vehicles
bio: Alasdair completed a degree in Geography and Environmental Science at Dundee in 2024, where a river restoration monitoring project sparked his interest in nature restoration. He then worked on river restoration projects in Scotland with River Revivers and founded his own restoration company, Alba Fiadhaich, which included a trial reintroduction of woodland wildflowers. He brings these experiences to his PhD at St Andrews.

name: Charlotte Sharpe
project: Meeting commitments to biodiversity conservation: predicting and monitoring the contributions of nature markets
bio: Charlotte's interests in ecology are broad, reflected in her past research. While studying biology and geography as a joint honours degree at St Andrews, she researched the evolutionary ecology of an uncommon form of seed dispersal (ballochory). In 2024 she moved to Durham to complete a more fieldwork-focused MRes involving the design and trial of novel camera trap devices for monitoring small mammals, alongside work on integrating citizen science and AI into camera trap image processing. She is currently fascinated by the gap between the UK's ambitious environmental policy and our ability to deliver on its end goals.

name: Joe O'Sullivan
project: Bundling benefits from peatlands to enable nature recovery
bio: Joe completed a BSc in Environmental Science at the University of Galway in 2022 and worked as an ecologist with Wetland Surveys Ireland, where he developed an interest in peatlands. In 2024 he began an MSc in Global Change: Ecosystem Science and Policy, a joint programme between University College Dublin and Justus Liebig University Giessen, with a thesis on water table monitoring in restored peatlands using drones. His PhD aims to design alternative funding approaches for recovering the UK's carbon-rich ecosystems, using bundled ecosystem health metrics and a mix of public and private funding.

name: Paul Muto
project: Safeguarding genetic integrity: provenance-based seed sourcing for Biodiversity Net Gain
bio: Paul has worked for many years across the agricultural and environmental sectors, with a particular interest in grasslands and their management. He is now a PhD researcher at Durham University, studying wildflower genetic diversity and the implications of Biodiversity Net Gain for habitat restoration. Using devil's-bit scabious as a model species, his research combines ddRAD sequencing and a common garden experiment to investigate differences among wild and commercially sourced populations and inform decisions about native seed sourcing.

name: Anna Wyeth
project: Private investment in Biodiversity Net Gain and its ability to deliver Local Nature Recovery Strategies
partner: Natural England, Durham County Council, Durham Wildlife Trust
bio: Anna has a background spanning geography, environmental science and ecology. Her MSc research at the Leverhulme Centre for Nature Recovery in Oxford examined eco-acoustics for monitoring soil health and macrofauna across grassland management, and she has social research experience on farmers' motivations for joining agri-environment schemes. Her interests include aligning policy and funding with local socio-ecological needs and interpreting the ecological effects of management decisions.

name: Viktor Wu
project: The marine rewilding effect: a cost-effective framework for measuring Marine Net Gain
bio: Viktor has a background in physical geography, focusing on geomatics and satellite remote sensing. He worked at the Swedish Board of Agriculture on a system for monitoring agricultural activity and as a research assistant in spatial statistics in Taiwan. He is interested in interactions between nature and society and pursues interdisciplinary research. His PhD builds a cost-effective framework for measuring marine rewilding using geospatial, bioacoustic and societal indicators.

name: Will Ashton
project: Bridging philosophy and ecology: ethical decision-making in wild salmonid conservation
bio: Will is a PhD student in Statistics at St Andrews working on applied statistical methods for ecological data. He holds a BSc in Biology and an MSc in Statistical Ecology, and his work addresses problems such as detectability, missing data and observer bias. He is interested in combining statistical methods with ethical tools to guide conservation decisions that are both data-driven and ethically informed.

name: Samana Tiwari
project: New nature markets at sea: evaluating stakeholder attitudes to guide policy and practice
bio: Samana is a PhD researcher in Environmental Geography at the University of Aberdeen. With a background in Geography and Environmental Science and a master's in Sustainability Transitions, she is passionate about finding practical ways to connect research with real-world impact. Outside of work she can usually be found with a cup of tea and a good book, or swimming.

name: Barnaby Fogg
project: Biodiversity Net Gain through nature restoration of urban green spaces
bio: Barnaby holds an MA in Zoology from the University of Cambridge and a Master of Land Economy from the University of Aberdeen, where his dissertation used media analysis to study conflict between farmers and the Cairngorms National Park Authority. Outside academia he volunteers as a ranger and as a leader for a community-owned woodland, and he is a birdwatcher, cook and musician. His PhD examines how urban nature restoration contributes to biodiversity and societal benefits.

name: Sarah Trebo
project: Socio-economic and ecological factors for successful island restoration across land and seascapes
bio: Sarah completed a BSc in Geography at the University of Aberdeen, then spent two years working outside academia, including at the Scottish Seabird Centre and the Firth of Forth Lobster Hatchery, which fuelled her interest in marine and island ecosystems. Her research interests span community views, human-nature relationships, habitat recovery and animal management.

name: Benjamin Heaney
project: A strategic, systems-based approach to the management of land predators in Scotland
bio: Ben's research interests are in quantitative ecology and ecological modelling. He gained an honours degree in Marine and Freshwater Biology at the University of Glasgow, studying two years of mathematics alongside it, and merged the two for his MSc thesis, also at Glasgow, constructing a novel mathematical framework to model and predict biomass change in a multi-species estuarine ecosystem contaminated with heavy metals. His PhD investigates the least destructive way to rearrange land use in Scotland to balance the fitness of land predators with the socio-economic benefits of the land to stakeholders. Outside academia he has worked as a bike mechanic, professional photographer and musician.

name: Stephen Martinelli
project: Nature credits for oyster aquaculture
bio: Stephen is from New York and previously worked on marine conservation and international policy with the Wildlife Conservation Society, The Pew Charitable Trusts and the US Peace Corps, focusing on marine protected areas. He holds a BSc in Economics from Wake Forest University and an MSc in Environmental Sciences and Policy from Johns Hopkins University, where he studied deep-sea mineral governance by the International Seabed Authority.

name: Cameron Potter
project: Trading places: how market design shapes landscapes and biodiversity
bio: Cameron completed his integrated master's degree in Zoology at the University of Glasgow in 2026. During it he worked as a consultant ecologist in Scotland, primarily on upland habitats, and researched the spatial distribution of new habitat created through Biodiversity Net Gain in England and its correlation with income. He also spent time at the Mpala Research Centre in Kenya and the Skalanes Nature and Heritage Centre in Iceland, gaining international experience on a range of research projects. He has always been passionate about interdisciplinary research and how it can be used to understand the relationship between societies and nature, which is what led him to his PhD with NETGAIN.

name: Christina Mazilu
project: Nature markets and the future of crofting in the Western Isles
partner: Galson Estate Trust, Community Land Outer Hebrides
bio: Christina completed an MA in Sociology at the University of Aberdeen in May 2025. Their final year project focused on how the policy process can engage or disengage communities and lead to action or inaction, through local council consultations, place-based policy frameworks and community-led decision-making, using participatory methods. Their PhD explores, together with crofting communities, the future of crofting within a net-zero and biodiversity-positive society, and what role nature markets for carbon and biodiversity could play in building sustainable pathways for culture and environment in rural Scotland.

name: Katerina Schiffnederova
project: The marine ecosystem net value of decommissioning offshore infrastructure
bio: Katerina completed a BSc in Marine Biology at the University of Essex and an MSc in Marine Ecosystem Management at the University of St Andrews, then returned to Essex for an MSD. Her research there, in collaboration with ZSL, SMASS and CSIP, examined spatiotemporal patterns of intentionally and unintentionally produced PCBs in harbour porpoises stranded around the British coast. Her PhD quantifies the ecosystem service cost of leaving cuttings piles and abandoned pipelines in place in the North Sea, and the net value of removing them, as an explicit basis for Nature Improvement Credits to offset decommissioning costs. She is a PGR board member of The Marine Biologist magazine and volunteers as a Marine Mammal Medic with British Divers Marine Life Rescue, so if you find a stranded animal on a beach walk, let her know. In her free time she enjoys nature walks with her dog Levi and travelling.

name: Charlie Willis
project: Finding the middle ground: balancing deer management, ecological recovery and traditional land use
bio: Charlie has a background spanning geography, environmental management, ecology and social science, with a focus on ecological monitoring for biodiversity conservation and sustainable land management in Scotland. His PhD examines how ecological non-linearities can help resolve conflict over land management, using the deer-biodiversity relationship as a case study.

name: George Koutsopoulos
project: Distilling the value of nature: integrated indicators for water, carbon and biodiversity
bio: George is originally from Greece, where he completed a BSc in Geology and Environmental Sciences at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, before moving to Italy for an MSc in Global Change Ecology and Sustainability at the University of Bologna. During his master's he undertook a research internship at the Norwegian Institute of Bioeconomy Research (NIBIO) in Tromsø, studying the eco-hydrology of mountain and Arctic springs through field measurements, hydrochemistry and ecological assessment. Having lived and studied in Greece, Italy and Norway, he has a strong interest in how ecosystems respond to environmental change across landscapes and climates. His PhD, based in the Blairfindy catchment at Glenlivet, investigates how nature-based solutions deliver interconnected benefits for water, carbon and biodiversity, and how those benefits can be measured and translated into indicators that support environmental investment. Outside academia he enjoys hiking, travelling, football and tennis.

name: Mercedes Mauriño Lascano
project: Biodiversity and soil health indicators to support high-integrity carbon credits in regenerative agriculture
bio: Mercedes is an environmental scientist from Argentina with a background in environmental chemistry, soil organic carbon modelling, and over a year of environmental monitoring work in Antarctica. Her PhD aims to make the environmental benefits of regenerative agriculture easier to verify, so that agricultural carbon credits reflect lasting changes in soil carbon, soil health and biodiversity.

name: Liliana Tarrant Snedden
project: Is 'complexity' the link between ecological function and the biodiversity metrics needed to deliver nature-positive outcomes?
bio: Liliana is a PhD student in Statistics at the University of St Andrews, applying mathematical theory to ecology to build practical conservation metrics and inform environmental policy. She has a background in Zoology (BSc) and statistical ecology (MRes) and describes herself as a true nature nerd, with a deep love of the natural world and an active curiosity about the workings of ecosystems, from soil mycelia to bird behaviour. She is driven by wanting to contribute to solutions to the climate and nature crises, and is passionate about the intersection of statistics, big data, practical conservation and environmental policy. Her PhD aims to develop tools to track ecosystem recovery using the theory of ecological complexity, supporting nature restoration, evidence-based policy and emerging nature markets.

name: Betsy Conger
project: Is there Net Gain in marine decommissioning? Rethinking the future and value of offshore infrastructure in the North Sea
bio: Betsy completed her BSc in Biology at Sewanee and MSc in Marine Ecosystem Management at the University of St Andrews, where her research focused on the impacts of marine heatwaves on rocky shore ecosystems in the Shetland Islands. She later worked as a Consents Intern at Ocean Winds, supporting offshore wind projects in the Moray Firth. She is now pursuing a PhD in Biology at St Andrews, exploring the intersection of marine ecosystems, offshore energy development and nature-positive approaches to marine management. Her PhD assesses the ecological value of offshore infrastructure and how that value can inform nature-positive decommissioning strategies and the delivery of Marine Net Gain.
